newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil profit-taking frenzy rocks regional markets.
newsitem.headline: Brazil profit-taking frenzy rocks regional markets.

text.p: Brazilian stocks tumbled Tuesday and took stock prices in other Latin American markets with them, dragged lower by profit-taking set off by fears of a currency devaluation.
Sao Paulo's Bovespa index of leading shares tumbled 1,081 points, or 8.51 percent, to 11,617, the biggest one-day drop in over two years.

Central bank officials denied plans for a devaluation, but rumours that Latin America's largest economy might allow its currency to fluctuate more freely sent shivers through financial markets in Argentina, Mexico and Venezuela, where investors look to Brazil -- not Wall Street -- for direction.
"It's difficult to say anything right now. Everybody wants to leave through the same door, that's why the market is plunging," said John Carioba, a trader at Indusval brokerage in Sao Paulo.
Despite the drop in the stock market, Brazil's currency, the real, resisted selling pressure and fell only slightly against the dollar.

Of all Latin American countries, Brazil is seen as the most likely to face a steep devaluation because of a growing trade gap, lax government spending controls and a currency that some observers say is overvalued by up to 20 percent, analysts and economists said.

Central bank officials denied any plans to devalue the currency or change the existing foreign exchange regime, which they defend with about $59 billion in foreign currency reserves. The central bank aims for a 7 percent to 8 percent depreciation of the real against the dollar a year, carried out through several mini-depreciations each month.

Economists played down the stock market's sell-off as exaggerated profit-taking after an unprecedented rally in Brazilian stocks, which have surged 80 percent so far this year. Investors and traders said a pullback was long overdue.
Economists noted that Brazil's economy, while not perfect, is in far better shape than Thailand's, for example, whose effective devaluation two weeks ago apparently started the rumours in Brazil.

"At this stage it's a healthy warning but not with the strength yet to have either systemic or contagion effects of substance," said Paulo Leme, senior international economist at Goldman Sachs and Co. in New York.

In Argentina, whose exports to Brazil would be seriously hurt by a Brazilian devaluation, the blue-chip MerVal stock index fell 3.37 percent. A cheaper real would make Brazilian exports more competitive in world markets.

Argentine Economy Minister Roque Fernandez, seeking to calm investor jitters, told a news conference in Washington that a sharp devaluation in Brazil was not in the works. He said the currency woes now plaguing Thailand, Indonesia and other Asian countries would not hurt Latin America.
In Mexico, stocks fell sharply and some traders referred to a "devaluation in Brazil" as though one had occurred.
